What Is Demand?

In economics, demand does not simply mean wanting something. It means being both willing and able to buy it. A teenager who wants a new games console but has no money is not contributing to demand in the economic sense — there is no “effective demand” unless the desire is backed by the purchasing power to act on it. Economists focus on this distinction because markets respond to spending, not wishes.

Demand is always for a good or service at a particular price, over a particular time period. When economists talk about “the demand for petrol”, they mean the total quantity all consumers are willing and able to purchase at each possible price, holding all other factors constant. This set of price–quantity relationships is captured in a demand schedule and drawn as a demand curve.

The Law of Demand

The central rule of demand is the law of demand: as the price of a good rises, the quantity demanded falls. As the price falls, the quantity demanded rises. The relationship between price and quantity demanded is inverse — they move in opposite directions.

Think about the petrol market. When fuel prices spike to 170p a litre, many drivers combine journeys, take public transport more often, or walk short distances they would normally drive. Fewer litres are bought. When prices fall to 130p, the same drivers fill up more readily and make trips they previously avoided. The quantity demanded rises. This behaviour is consistent and predictable across virtually every market.

There are two reasons why demand behaves this way. First, as a good becomes more expensive it also becomes expensive relative to alternatives, so consumers switch to substitutes — this is the substitution effect. Second, a price rise reduces the real purchasing power of a consumer’s income, so they can afford to buy less overall — this is the income effect. Both effects push quantity demanded in the same direction: downwards when price rises.

Key Fact

The demand curve slopes downward from left to right because of the law of demand: higher prices reduce quantity demanded (substitution effect + income effect). A demand curve is drawn with price on the vertical axis and quantity demanded on the horizontal axis.

Movement Along the Demand Curve

A change in the price of the good itself causes a movement along the demand curve. If petrol rises from 140p to 160p per litre, consumers move up the demand curve to a lower quantity demanded. If it falls to 120p, they move down to a higher quantity. The curve itself does not move — only the position of the consumer on it changes.

It is important to use precise language here. A rise in price causes a contraction of demand — less is demanded. A fall in price causes an extension of demand — more is demanded. Examiners expect you to use these terms rather than simply saying demand “goes up” or “goes down” when the price changes.

Students frequently write that a price rise “decreases demand”. This is technically incorrect and can cost marks. When price changes, the demand curve stays fixed — only the quantity demanded changes, shown as a movement along the existing curve. The correct phrasing is: a price rise causes a contraction of demand (a fall in quantity demanded). A price fall causes an extension of demand (a rise in quantity demanded). Reserve the phrase “demand increases” or “demand decreases” for when the whole curve shifts due to a non-price factor.

Shifts in the Demand Curve

A shift in the demand curve happens when a factor other than price changes. The whole curve moves — at every possible price, consumers now want a different quantity. A rightward shift means more is demanded at every price; a leftward shift means less is demanded at every price. The factors that cause shifts are sometimes called the conditions of demand.

To picture this: imagine petrol demand before and after a 20% rise in household incomes. At every price point, drivers are now willing to buy more fuel — they take more car journeys, use the car for shorter trips, and are less sensitive to cost. The entire demand curve shifts to the right. Price has not changed; the conditions of demand have changed.

Key Fact

The main factors that shift the demand curve are: income, tastes and fashion, the prices of related goods, population and demographics, advertising, and interest rates or credit availability. A rightward shift shows a rise in demand; a leftward shift shows a fall in demand.

Factors That Shift Demand

Income. For most goods (called normal goods), a rise in income shifts the demand curve to the right. People buy more holidays, restaurant meals and new clothes when they earn more. For a small category of goods (called inferior goods), demand actually falls as income rises — for example, demand for budget own-brand foods tends to fall when incomes improve, as consumers trade up to branded alternatives.

Tastes and fashion. Consumer preferences change over time. The rise of plant-based diets shifted the demand curve for meat alternatives sharply to the right through the 2010s. Meanwhile, demand for physical DVDs shifted to the left as streaming services became dominant. Advertising and social media trends can accelerate these changes in taste rapidly.

Prices of related goods. Two goods can be related as substitutes or complements. If the price of bus fares rises sharply, demand for cars may increase — consumers switch from one mode of transport to the other. If the price of car insurance rises steeply, demand for cars themselves may fall, because the total cost of motoring has risen even though the car’s own price is unchanged.

Population. A larger population, or a change in its age structure, shifts demand. An ageing population, for instance, increases demand for healthcare, mobility aids and retirement housing. A rising number of young adults increases demand for rented accommodation and entry-level smartphones.

Advertising. Effective advertising changes consumer preferences, shifting the demand curve to the right for the advertised product. When a supermarket runs a major promotional campaign for its own-brand products, demand at every price point may rise.

The most common mistake in demand questions is confusing these two. Ask yourself: What has changed? If the answer is the good’s own price, you have a movement along the curve — either an extension (price falls, quantity demanded rises) or a contraction (price rises, quantity demanded falls). If the answer is anything else — income, tastes, prices of other goods, population, advertising — you have a shift of the whole curve. A rightward shift means demand has increased; a leftward shift means demand has decreased. Examiners mark this distinction very precisely.

A Worked Example

Consider the market for electric vehicles (EVs). Suppose manufacturers cut the price of a popular EV model from £35,000 to £28,000. The fall in the good’s own price causes an extension of demand — a movement down the demand curve to a higher quantity. This is a movement along the existing curve; the curve itself does not move. At the same time, a high-profile advertising campaign promotes the environmental benefits of EVs, changing consumer tastes in favour of them. This causes a rightward shift of the entire demand curve. Both changes increase the quantity of EVs demanded, but they work through different mechanisms and would be shown differently on a demand diagram: the price cut is a movement along the curve; the advertising campaign is a shift of the curve.

Why Markets Are Linked

No market exists in isolation. When the price of petrol rises, demand for electric cars tends to increase. When the price of coffee falls, demand for coffee machines may rise. When farmers grow more wheat, the supply of straw — a by-product — also rises. These links between markets are called intermarket relationships, and understanding them is essential for predicting how prices and quantities adjust across the economy.

Substitute Goods

Substitute goods are goods that compete with each other. Butter and margarine are substitutes — if the price of butter rises sharply, consumers switch to margarine, so the demand for margarine increases. On a demand curve, this looks like a rightward shift in the demand for margarine: at every price, more margarine is now demanded. The equilibrium price of margarine rises and more is sold.

You can see this in the UK streaming market. When one major streaming service raises its monthly subscription price, consumers shop around and sign up for rival services instead. The demand curve for the rival shifts to the right — more subscribers at every price — pushing that rival’s equilibrium price up and its quantity of subscribers higher.

Key Fact

For substitute goods: if the price of Good A rises, demand for substitute Good B shifts RIGHT — raising the equilibrium price and quantity of B. The two markets move in the SAME direction for price.

Complementary Goods

Complementary goods are goods consumed jointly. Printers and printer ink are complements — you can’t use one without the other. If the price of printers falls dramatically, more printers are sold, and so demand for printer ink rises too. The demand curve for printer ink shifts to the right, raising the equilibrium price and quantity of ink.

Think about petrol and cars. If petrol prices rise sharply and stay high, the cost of running a car goes up. Consumers may delay buying new cars or switch to smaller, more fuel-efficient models. Demand for large petrol-engine cars shifts left — lower price and fewer sold. The two goods are complements, so their markets move in OPPOSITE directions: petrol up, car demand down.

Key Fact

For complementary goods: if the price of Good A rises, demand for complement Good B shifts LEFT — reducing the equilibrium price and quantity of B. The two markets move in OPPOSITE directions for quantity sold.

Students often confuse substitutes and complements. The test is simple: can you use one instead of the other (substitute), or do you need both together (complement)?

For substitutes, a price rise in one good INCREASES demand for the other — the demand curves move in the same direction. For complements, a price rise in one good DECREASES demand for the other — the demand curves move in opposite directions. In both cases, the mechanism is a shift in the demand curve, not a movement along it; the consumers’ preferences or the conditions of demand have changed.

Derived Demand

Derived demand occurs when the demand for one good comes from the demand for something else. Steel is demanded not because consumers enjoy steel for its own sake, but because firms need it to build cars, bridges and appliances. If the demand for new cars rises — say, because consumer confidence improves — car manufacturers need more steel and the demand for steel rises too. The demand curve for steel shifts to the right, raising steel prices and output.

Derived demand is also central to the labour market. A building company hires bricklayers not for their own sake but to build houses. If house prices rise and the property market booms, more houses are commissioned, demand for bricklayers rises, and wages in the construction sector are pushed up. The demand for labour is always a derived demand — it flows from the demand for the final product or service.

Composite Demand

Composite demand arises when a good is demanded for more than one purpose. Milk is a classic example: it is demanded for drinking, for making cheese, for making butter and for producing yoghurt. If demand for cheese rises sharply — perhaps because a health trend promotes high-protein diets — more milk is diverted to cheese production. Less milk is available for other uses, so the price of drinking milk and butter rises too. A single resource being pulled in different directions creates competition between those uses.

Land illustrates composite demand clearly. Farmland is demanded for growing crops, for building houses and for renewable energy projects such as solar farms. When house-building programmes expand, more land is bid away from agriculture. This reduces the supply of land for farming, pushing up the cost of growing food and ultimately raising food prices.

Joint supply (also called joint production) occurs when producing one good necessarily produces another as a by-product. Beef and leather are the classic example: both come from cattle. If the demand for beef rises, farmers rear more cattle, and the supply of leather increases automatically. On a supply-and-demand diagram, the supply of leather shifts to the right, reducing the equilibrium price of leather and increasing the quantity sold.

The North Sea oil industry provides a further example: crude oil extraction yields natural gas as a by-product. When oil production increases, the supply of natural gas rises too, even if the demand for gas has not changed. This can depress gas prices and affect the profitability of gas producers.

Competitive supply occurs when two goods compete for the same limited resources. A farmer with a fixed area of land must choose between growing wheat or oilseed rape. If the price of wheat rises, it becomes more profitable to grow wheat. The farmer switches land from oilseed rape to wheat, so the supply of oilseed rape falls — its supply curve shifts left and its price rises. The two markets move in opposite directions for quantity supplied.

How a Change in One Market Ripples Through Others

Real-world economic events rarely stay confined to a single market. Consider what happened when global semiconductor shortages emerged after 2020. Semiconductors are in composite demand — they are used in cars, laptops, fridges, smartphones and medical equipment. When supply fell sharply, prices rose across all these markets. Car manufacturers were forced to pause production lines because they could not obtain the chips they needed (derived demand at work: fewer chips → fewer cars). Meanwhile, rival producers of less chip-intensive goods gained a competitive edge as consumers switched to alternatives (substitute goods at work).

Tracing these chains is exactly what examiners want to see: identify the initial change, state how it affects the demand or supply curve in the first market, then follow the ripple into linked markets, naming the relationship type (substitute, complement, joint supply, competitive supply or derived demand) at each step.

What Is Supply?

Supply is the amount of a good or service that producers are willing and able to sell at each possible price. Notice those two words: “willing” means producers want to sell, and “able” means they can actually produce and deliver it. A farmer who wants to sell 1,000 tonnes of wheat but can only harvest 200 tonnes is “able” to supply just 200 tonnes, regardless of willingness.

Supply is always measured over a specific time period — for example, the number of loaves a bakery can supply per week, or the number of cars a manufacturer can produce per month. Supply and price are closely linked: in most markets, the higher the price, the more producers want to supply.

The Law of Supply

The law of supply states that there is a positive relationship between price and quantity supplied, all other things being equal. Think about a coffee shop: if the price of a cup of coffee rises from £3 to £4.50, the owner has a stronger incentive to brew and sell more cups — the higher price covers costs more easily and leaves a larger profit on every sale. Conversely, if the price falls, it may no longer be worth producing as much, so the quantity supplied contracts.

The phrase “all other things being equal” (often written as the Latin ceteris paribus) is vital. It means we are changing only the price and holding everything else — technology, input costs, taxes — constant. In the real world, several things change at once, which is why we study each factor separately.

Key Fact

The law of supply: as price rises, quantity supplied rises; as price falls, quantity supplied falls — ceteris paribus. This gives the supply curve its upward slope.

The Supply Curve

Economists draw a supply curve on a graph with price on the vertical axis (P) and quantity supplied on the horizontal axis (Q). Because of the law of supply, this curve slopes upward from left to right. At a low price, producers supply a small quantity; at a high price, they supply a large quantity. Each point on the curve represents one price–quantity combination.

For example, a clothing manufacturer might supply 5,000 jackets per week when each jacket sells for £40, but 9,000 jackets per week when the price rises to £70. If you plotted these pairs on a graph, the curve connecting them would rise as you move to the right — higher price, higher quantity supplied.

This is one of the most common sources of confusion in GCSE Economics. A movement along the supply curve happens when only the price of the good changes. If the price rises, producers move up the existing curve, supplying more — this is called an extension of supply. If the price falls, they move down the existing curve, supplying less — a contraction of supply.

A shift in the supply curve happens when something other than the price of the good changes — for example, production costs fall, or new technology is introduced. This shifts the entire curve: a shift to the RIGHT means more is supplied at every price (an increase in supply); a shift to the LEFT means less is supplied at every price (a decrease in supply).

The key test: if the change is caused by a price change, it’s a movement. If it’s caused by anything else, it’s a shift.

Factors That Shift the Supply Curve

Several non-price factors can shift the supply curve to the left or right. The most important are costs of production, technology, taxes, subsidies, weather or natural factors, the number of firms in the market, and the productivity of factors of production.

1. Costs of Production

Costs of production are the expenses firms face when making their product. If costs rise — for instance, if the price of steel rises for a car manufacturer, or if energy bills double for a bakery — it becomes more expensive to produce each unit. Firms respond by supplying less at every price, so the supply curve shifts LEFT. Conversely, if costs fall (perhaps because wages fall or cheaper raw materials become available), firms can profitably supply more, shifting the curve RIGHT.

2. Technology

Improvements in technology allow firms to produce the same output with fewer inputs, lowering the cost per unit. A car manufacturer that introduces robotic assembly lines can produce more vehicles per day than a fully manual production line — reducing unit costs and increasing supply at every price. Technological improvements typically shift the supply curve to the RIGHT.

Key Fact

Supply shifts RIGHT (increases) when: costs fall, technology improves, a subsidy is granted, more firms enter the market, productivity rises, or (for agricultural goods) weather is favourable. Supply shifts LEFT (decreases) when: costs rise, a tax is imposed, firms leave the market, or bad weather destroys a harvest.

3. Taxes and Subsidies

Government intervention directly affects supply. An indirect tax on production (such as an environmental levy on a factory’s carbon emissions) adds to the firm’s costs, making production more expensive and shifting supply LEFT. A subsidy, on the other hand, is a financial payment from the government that reduces production costs. For example, a government subsidy for solar panel manufacturers lowers their costs, allowing them to supply more panels at every price, shifting supply RIGHT.

4. Weather and Natural Factors

For primary-sector goods — particularly agricultural products like wheat, coffee, and cocoa — weather has a major influence on supply. A warm, dry summer and plentiful rainfall can produce a bumper harvest, shifting the supply curve RIGHT and driving prices down. A frost, drought, or disease (such as a coffee leaf-rust outbreak) destroys crops, shifting supply LEFT and pushing prices up. This is why food prices can be volatile from year to year.

5. Number of Firms and Productivity

Two further non-price factors shift the supply curve. First, the number of firms in a market: if new producers enter, total market supply increases and the supply curve shifts RIGHT. If firms exit — for example, because the market becomes unprofitable — market supply falls and the curve shifts LEFT. Second, productivity: if workers or machines become more efficient, each unit of output requires fewer inputs, lowering unit costs. Higher productivity therefore shifts the supply curve to the RIGHT, just as a fall in input costs does.

An extension of supply occurs when the price of the good rises and producers supply a greater quantity as a result — this is a movement UP the supply curve. A contraction of supply occurs when the price of the good falls and producers supply a smaller quantity — a movement DOWN the curve. Both are movements, not shifts. In your exam, examiners deduct marks if you call a movement a “shift” — the distinction matters.

A quick memory trick: if the word “price” appears in the explanation, it’s a movement. If any other word appears (costs, tax, subsidy, weather, technology), it’s a shift.

Why Supply Matters to Producers and Consumers

Understanding supply helps explain real-world price changes. When droughts cut cocoa yields in West Africa, chocolate manufacturers face higher input costs and lower raw-material availability — supply falls, and the price of chocolate rises. When a new semiconductor factory opens and chips become cheaper to make, the supply of smartphones and laptops increases, putting downward pressure on prices. Supply-side changes ripple through the entire market, affecting the price consumers pay and the profit producers earn.
